div.p: Real-time knowledgebased systems @Ss) are increasingly used to monitor and control real-time processes.

Although a KBS may perform well on the average in terms of computation time, it may fail to deliver results while meeting deadlines in some critical cases. This is not acceptable in a hard real-time system where all liming constraints imposed by the environment must be continuously observed by the embedded computer and the failure to meet a single deadline may be catastrophic. Thus the technology for building a new generation of real-time KBSs must be developed before we can rely on these smart systems to perform complex, safety-critical. monitoring and control functions in a real-time environment as we currently do on embedded software programs implemented in procedural languages. In this article, we examine some fundamental issues in the design and development of realtime KBSs including (1) response time analysis, and ( 2) rule-base optimization and synthesis. * This material is b e d upon work supported in paa by the National Science Foundation uoda Award No. CCR-9111563 and by Ihe Texap Advanad Research Program under Grant No. 3652270.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: There is a rapid increase in the use of embedded computers in time-critical systems ranging from the anti-lock braking controller in automobiles to the on-board safety mechanism in the Space Shuttle. The ability of these realtime monitoring and control computers to deliver results on time becomes as important as the abiiity of such computers to deliver correct results whenever needed. Since these embedded computers are used to perform increasingly complex monitoring, diagnosis, and control functions, realtime knowledge-based expert systems (KBSs) are becoming increasingly popular in the implementation of these embedded computer systems [lo]. Otber emerging motivations for employing KBSs include the increasing complexity of operations performed by the system being monitored and controlled, the repetitive nature of the monitoring and control functions which ais0 i m p e very short time for computer response, the unavailability of efficient deterministic algorithms for solving the real-time decision problems which are more amenable to rule-based reasoning, and a rapidly changing environment requiring learning and adaptive capabilities.

Real-time KBSs are embedded artj6cial intelligence (AI) systems which must respond to the environment being monitored and controlled within stringent timing constraints. They are programs which encode applicationspecific knowledge expressed in the form of $--then rules.

Based on input sensor values, the embedded KBS must make decisions within bounded time to respond to the external environmenc the result of missing a deadline may be catastrophic. Thus a real-time KBS makes critical decisions that are used to uarantee the safety and progress of the environment in wiich they are embedded. However, these decisions are only useful if they are produced within the timing constraints imposed by the environment. There fore, it is required not only to verify the logical correctness of a real-time expert system but also to determine whether the computation time required to compute a logically COTrect deciiion in each monitor-decide cycle is within the imposed riming constraint Thi added complexity of timing requirements makes the design and maintenance of these systems particularly difficult.

Although a KBS may perform well on the average in terms of computation time, it may fail to deliver results whiie meeting deadlines in some critical cases. In fat& the performance of a KBS is highly unpredictable in a realme environment owing to the fact that the control flow of the NI= in these systems is embedded io the data and cannot be easily deduced [ 113. l%is is not acceptable in a hard real-time system (as in the case of the anti-lock braking controller or the Space Shuttle safety mechanism) where the failure to meet a single deadline may be catastrophic. There have been few attempts to formalize the question of whether rule-based systems can deliver adequate performance in bounded time. Thus the technology for building the next generation of real-time KBSs must be developed before we can rely on these smart systems to perform complex monitoring and control functions in a real-time environment as we currently do on software programs imple mented in procedural languages such as C and C++. We examine some fundamental issues in the design and development of real-time KBSs in this paper, including respunse time analysis, and rule-base optimization and synthesis.

Past research focused only on performance analysis and optimization of KBSs for sofi real-time applications, where the failure to meet some timing constraints can be tolerated We begin this article by describing some basic features of real-time KBSs. For motivation, a small example rulebase written in EQL is given. Then we show how to represent and visualize the execution of a KBS using a state space graph. Next we discuss the response time analysis problem and the rule-base optimization/synthesis problem. Ractical solutions for these fundamental problems are outlined and examples are given to demonstrate their capabilities. Finally, the conclusion ends this article with some relevant remarks.

div.head: Real-Time Rule-Based Program
div.p: In general, the analysis problem to determine whether a rule-based program will reach a fixed point is undecidable if the program variables can have infinite domains, i.e., there is no general procedure for answering all instances of the decision problem 121. To get a better handle on this complex problem, we shall use a simpler rule-based language to study the analysis problem so that we can concentrate on the problem itself and not on the complexity of the language. This simpler language is called EQL (Equational Logic rulebased language) which has been extended to MRL (macro rule-based language) [11] EQL differs from OPS5 and other popular expert system languages in some important ways. These differences reflect the goal of our research, which is not to invent yet another expert system shell but to investigate whether and how perfomance objectives can be met when rule-based programs are used to perform safety-critical functions in real time. whereas the interpretation of a language like OPS5 is defined by the recognizeact cycle [5], the basic interpretation cycle of EQL is defined by fixed point convergence. It is our belief that the time it takes to converge to a fixed point is a more pertinent measure of the response time of a rulebased program than the length of the m gnize-act cycle. More importantly, we do not require the firing of rules that lead to a fixed point to be implemented sequentially. Rules can be 6red in parallel if they do not interfere with one another [31. The definition of response time in terms of fixed point convergence is architecture independent and is therefore more robust.

The RULES section of an EQL program is composed of a finite set of rules of the form: (1) VAR: the left-hand-side variables of the multiple assignment statement, i.e., the ai's, (2) VAL: the right-hand-side expressions of the multiple assignment statement, i.e., the bi s, and (3) EC: the enabling condition.

An enabling condition is a predicate on the variables in the program. A rule is enabled if its enabling condition becomes true. A rule firing is the execution of the multiple assignment statement. A rule is jrable only when it is enabled and if by firing it will change the value of some variable in VAR. A multiple assignment statement assigns values to one or more variables in parallel. The VAL expressions must be side-effect free. The execution of a multiple assignment statement consists of the evaluation of all the VAL expressions, followed by updating the VAR variables with the values of the corresponding expressions. An invocation of an EQL program is a sequence of rule firings. When two or more rules ~IE enabled, the selection of which rule to fire is nondeterministic or up to the run-time scheduler. An EQL program is said to have reached a $xed point when none of its rules is firable. An EQL program is said to always reach a fixed point in bounded rime if and only if the number of rule firings needed to take the program from an initial state to a fixed point is always bounded by a fixed upper bound imposed by environmental constraints. It is possible that a program can reach different fixed points starting from the same initial state, depending on which and how rules are fired. This may suggest that the correctness of the program is violated, whereas for some applications this is acceptable. Our coocun in this article is, however, on designing KBSs that meet the specified timing requirements.

EQL is an equational rule-based langyge which we have implemented to run under BSD UNIX . where xi is a value in the domain of the i" input sensor variable and si is a value in the domain of the j" internal variable. A rule is enabled at vertex i if and only if its enabling condition is satisfied by the tuple of variable values at vertex i. Each edge denotes the firing of a rule such that an edge (i, j ) connects vertex i to vertex j if and only if there is a rule r which is enabled at vertex i, and firing r will modify the program variables to have the same values as the tuple at vertex j . Obviously, if the domains of all the variables in a program are finite, then the corresponding state space graph must be finite. Note that the state space graph of a program need not be connected.

In this article, the timing constraint of interest is a deadline which must be met by every monitor-decide cycle of an EQL program. In terms of the state space representation, the timing constraint imposes an upper bound on the length of paths from a launch state to a fixed point.

div.head: Rule Base Optimization and Synthesis
div.p: Once a KBS is found to violate the specified timing constraints, then an optimization-synthesis (OS) transformation should be applied to the KBS to yield another KBS (with the same functionality) which meets the specified Wing constraints. Solutions to the OS problem are not in general polynomial time. Determining whether a scheduler exists which meets a response time constraint is also NPhard. A general, application-independent approach is to tackle the problem incrementally using a state space graph (SSG) introduced earlier or a rule transition graph (RTG) representation of the KBS to be optimized. F i t EQL KBSs with boolean variables are considered. Then the technique will be extended to KBSs with multi-valued variables and structured/pattern variables. Both the number of rule hings and the time for each match will be considered. The outline of this approach is as follows: [l] Given a KBS that does not meet the specified timiig constraints, construct the corresponding SSG or RTG. [2] Perform computations on the SSG or the RTG to obtain required values for optimization such as shortest paths and cycles to be broken.

[3] Modify the SSG or the RTG using an optimizing procedure and the above values to obtain a new SSG or RTG. Techniques such as the application of heuristic search, logic minimization, neural networks, and simulated annealing are applied as appropriate.

[4] Synthesize a new KBS from the modified graph(s); this KBS is guaranteed to always reach a fixed point withi rhe specified time period. Each of the steps of this OS methodology constitutes a nonuivial problem which must be resolved before we can apply it to optimie programs that meet both the timing constraints as well as the integrity constraints. Next, we describe an approach based on state space graphs [121.
Due to space limitations, we describe the optimization of EQL programs with boolean variables only here.

div.p: We then synthesize new nile-based programs from tbe modified graphs. div.head: Conclusion
div.p: The main focus of this article is to address the design issues of real-time KBSs.
